div.p: Q: What should the app do for users during a flood event? (Select all that apply) A: Show flood risk predictions on a map, Connect people to emergency resources (shelters, food, rescue), Send personalized alerts & evacuation routes, Track & learn from reported flood conditions
Q: Who is the primary user of this app? A: General public / residents
Q: What should we build right now? A: Interactive dashboard (map + risk + resources)

div.p: Here's your FloodGuard interactive dashboard! Here's what's built in and how it connects to your existing flood prediction model:

ul.class: [li_&]:mb-0 [li_&]:mt-1 [li_&]:gap-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ul]:pb-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ol]:pb-1 list-disc flex flex-col gap-1 pl-8 mb-3
ul.li: Clickable risk zones (A–F) on the map — each shows flood probability, population, and recommended action
Live alerts panel with 3 severity levels (emergency, warning, watch)
24h risk forecast bar chart (red/amber/green by threshold)
Emergency resource finder with real-time capacity status
Community condition reporting form (road flooding, power outages, rescue requests)
Time slider to scrub through 72h forecast — updates rainfall and river stage readouts
Animated river with evacuation route overlay

div.p: How to plug in your model: The map zones each have a prob field (flood probability 0–100%). You'd replace those with real-time predictions from your model's output. Same with m-rain, m-stage, and riskData[] in the chart — those would pipe from your data layer.

ol.class: [li_&]:mb-0 [li_&]:mt-1 [li_&]:gap-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ul]:pb-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ol]:pb-1 list-decimal flex flex-col gap-1 pl-8 mb-3
ol.li: AI chatbot panel — residents can ask "is my address safe?" and get a personalized answer using your model + Claude API
SMS/push alert integration — trigger alerts when a zone's predicted probability crosses a threshold
Crowd-sourced learning loop — submitted reports feed back into your model as ground-truth validation
Historical comparison — "this flood vs. 2019" side panel

div.p: Want me to build any of these features, or wire up the API integration with your actual model data?

div.h2: Claude responded: Great idea — a chatbot is one of the most impactful things you can add for residents during a crisis.

div.p: Great idea — a chatbot is one of the most impactful things you can add for residents during a crisis. Here are the main ways to implement it:

Approach 1: Claude API-powered chatbot (recommended) Embed a chat widget that calls the Anthropic API with a custom system prompt tailored to flood emergencies. The system prompt would include your local resource data (shelter addresses, hotlines, evacuation routes) and instruct Claude to be calm, empathetic, and action-oriented. This gives you the most natural, emotionally intelligent responses with zero ML training on your end. Since you're already building in this environment, this is the fastest path.

Approach 2: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Your chatbot retrieves relevant chunks from a knowledge base (FEMA guides, local emergency plans, your flood prediction data) before generating a response. Best when you have a large, structured document library and want answers grounded strictly in your official sources. More engineering overhead but highly accurate.

Approach 3: Rule-based + LLM hybrid High-priority intents (e.g. "I need rescue," "where is the nearest shelter") are handled by deterministic rules that instantly return structured data. Everything else falls through to the LLM. This gives you reliability for life-safety queries and flexibility for open-ended emotional support.

Approach 4: Fine-tuned smaller model Train a smaller model specifically on flood-related conversations and your local data. Lower cost at scale, works offline. But requires labeled training data and significant ML work — probably overkill for a first version.

hr.p: For your use case, Approach 1 or 3 makes the most sense. The system prompt is doing the heavy lifting: it tells Claude who it is, what resources are available, and how to balance emotional support with practical action.
Want me to build the chatbot widget right now using the Claude API? I can wire it directly into the dashboard with:

div.h2: Claude responded: Really important question — and a great one to raise at a hackathon.

div.p: Really important question — and a great one to raise at a hackathon. Here's how to think about it:
The core tension: Residents share sensitive emotional state and location data with the chatbot → emergency agents need that info to help → but users must trust the system or they won't use it at all.
Here's what you'd implement across three layers:

1. Data minimization (collect only what's needed) Don't store full conversation transcripts. Instead, extract only structured summaries — "User in Zone B, reports anxiety, requested shelter info, no rescue needed." The raw emotional language never persists. This is the single biggest privacy win and it's easy to demo.

2. Consent + transparency at the start of every chat The chatbot opens with something like: "Your conversation helps us connect you with the right resources. Agents may see a summary if you need urgent help. Nothing is shared without your knowledge." One tap to agree. This builds trust and is legally defensible.

3. Role-based access for agents Agents don't see raw chat — they see a structured triage card: risk level, zone, needs flagged, consent given. Only a supervisor or rescue coordinator can escalate to see more detail, and that access is logged. Think of it like a hospital triage system — the nurse sees your vitals, the doctor sees your chart, the receptionist sees your name.

4. Encryption + session scoping Chats are encrypted in transit and at rest. Each session gets a temporary ID — not tied to a real identity unless the user voluntarily shares it (name, address). Sessions expire after the event window.

hr.p: For the hackathon specifically, you don't need to build all of this — you need to demonstrate that you've thought through it. Here's your winning answer:
Want me to build a quick visual that shows the data flow — from user chat → anonymization → agent triage card — that you can include in your pitch deck or demo?

div.h2: Claude responded: Option 3 — Consent banner + structured triage card.

div.p: Option 3 — Consent banner + structured triage card. It's the easiest to build, looks the most impressive in a demo, and directly answers the "how do you protect users?" question judges always ask.
Here's exactly what you build:

ol.class: [li_&]:mb-0 [li_&]:mt-1 [li_&]:gap-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ul]:pb-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ol]:pb-1 list-decimal flex flex-col gap-1 pl-8 mb-3
ol.li: Consent message at the start of the chat — one sentence, one button. Done in 10 minutes.

The chatbot extracts a structured summary instead of storing raw chat — you just add a line to your Claude system prompt like "After each conversation, output a JSON summary with: zone, needs, emotional_state, consent_given." Done in 5 minutes.
An agent triage card that displays that JSON in a clean UI — name, zone, needs flagged, risk level. Agents see this, not the raw conversation. Done in 30 minutes.

div.p: That's it. Total build time: under an hour. And in your demo you can show:

The bot responding with empathy + resources →
An agent dashboard showing only the clean triage card →
And say "the raw conversation never persists"

div.p: Click any box to learn more about that step. Here's the breakdown:

Is Mastra respected? Yes — it scored 9/10 for developer experience vs LangChain's 5/10, and is built on top of Vercel's AI SDK. It's open source under Apache 2.0 and built by the team behind Gatsby, so it has real pedigree. Generative, Inc.GitHub

p.strong: How it works for your chatbot:

div.p: Mastra is an open-source TypeScript agent framework — you can use it to build AI agents that have memory, execute tools, or chain LLM calls in deterministic workflows. For your flood chatbot specifically: DEV Community

ul.class: [li_&]:mb-0 [li_&]:mt-1 [li_&]:gap-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ul]:pb-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ol]:pb-1 list-disc flex flex-col gap-1 pl-8 mb-3
ul.li: Your EmotionalTriageAgent detects distress signals in the message and decides whether to prioritize resources or emotional support first
A ResourceLookupTool pulls real shelter/hotline data based on the user's zone
Both feed into the Claude API call with a pre-built system prompt

div.p: API call transparency — this is the key part for your hackathon. Mastra has built-in tracing of agent calls and token usage, with support for your own observability platform. That means every single API call — what prompt was sent, what Claude replied, how many tokens, how long it took — is automatically logged. You can show judges a live trace panel and say "here's exactly what was sent to the AI and what came back." No black box. Mastra

div.h2: Claude responded: Got it!

div.p: Got it! Here's exactly what you need to install and set up before writing any code:

1. Install Flutter SDK Go to flutter.dev/docs/get-started/install, pick your OS (Windows/Mac/Linux), and follow the steps. It installs the Flutter CLI and Dart together — you don't install Dart separately.

2. Install Android Studio This gives you the Android emulator + the Android SDK. During setup make sure to also install the Android Virtual Device (AVD) so you can run the app on a simulated phone. If you're on a Mac and want to test on iPhone too, you'll also need Xcode from the App Store.

3. Install VS Code (recommended for hackathon speed) Then install two extensions inside VS Code: "Flutter" and "Dart" — both by the Dart Code team. These give you hot reload, widget previews, and error highlighting.
4. Run flutter doctor After installing, open your terminal and run:

div.h2: Claude responded: Yes — VS Code alone doesn't include Flutter.

div.p: Yes — VS Code alone doesn't include Flutter. You need to install Flutter separately. Here's the quickest way:
1. Download Flutter SDK Go to flutter.dev/docs/get-started/install, pick your OS, and download the Flutter SDK zip. Extract it somewhere like C:\flutter on Windows or ~/flutter on Mac.
2. Add Flutter to your PATH So your terminal can find the flutter command. On Mac add this to your ~/.zshrc:

div.class: relative group/copy bg-bg-000/50 border-0.5 border-border-400 rounded-lg focus:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-accent-100
sticky opacity-0 group-hover/copy:opacity-100 group-focus-within/copy:opacity-100 top-2 py-2 h-12 w-0 float-right
absolute right-0 h-8 px-2 items-center inline-flex z-10

button.class: inline-flex items-center justify-center relative isolate shrink-0 can-focus select-none disabled:pointer-events-none disabled:opacity-50 disabled:shadow-none disabled:drop-shadow-none border-transparent transition font-base duration-300 ease-[cubic-bezier(0.165,0.85,0.45,1)] h-8 w-8 rounded-md backdrop-blur-md _fill_10ocf_9 _ghost_10ocf_96

div.style: width: 20px; height: 20px; display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
width: 20px; height: 20px; display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;

pre.style: color: rgb(20, 24, 31); background: transparent; font-family: var(--font-mono);

code.style: color: rgb(20, 24, 31); background: transparent; font-family: var(--font-mono); white-space: pre-wrap;

div.p: On Windows, add the flutter\bin folder to your system Environment Variables.
3. Install the Flutter + Dart extensions in VS Code Open VS Code → Extensions (Ctrl+Shift+X) → search "Flutter" → install the one by Dart Code. It automatically installs Dart too.

4. Install Android Studio You need this even if you don't use it as your editor — Flutter needs the Android SDK and emulator that come with it. When installing, make sure to check "Android Virtual Device" so you get a phone emulator.
5. Check everything works Open your terminal in VS Code and run:

That's the full setup. The whole thing takes about 20–30 minutes depending on your internet speed since Android Studio downloads are large. Want me to start on the code once you're set up?

span.span: // Build system prompt with live flood context

code.span: You are FloodGuard, a calm and empathetic flood safety assistant.
You are helping a resident during an active flood emergency.
1. Always acknowledge the person's feelings BEFORE giving resources.
2. Never minimize their fear — validate it first.
3. Be concise. People in emergencies don't read long messages.
4. If they mention physical danger or needing rescue, immediately give 911 and the rescue hotline: 541-FLOOD-01.
5. End every response with one clear next action.
At the END of every response, append a JSON block (hidden from user display) like this:

span.span: // Build conversation history for the API
// Split visible reply from hidden triage JSON

div.h2: Claude responded: Great question!

div.p: Great question! So .dart is Flutter's own language — here's the simple breakdown:
Flutter uses Dart — it's the only language for the app itself. You can't mix React or JavaScript inside a Flutter app. Dart is what powers everything — the UI, the logic, the API calls, all of it.
But here's the good news — Dart feels very similar to languages you might already know:

p.strong: So your stack for FloodGuard would look like this:

code.span: Claude API (HTTP) ← your chatbot, called from Dart
Your flood model ← Python/whatever you built it in, runs on a server
Mastra (TypeScript) ← agent workflow, runs as a backend API

div.p: The key insight: React/TypeScript/Python don't go inside the Flutter app — they live on the backend as APIs. Flutter just calls them over HTTP. So your team can split the work:

ul.class: [li_&]:mb-0 [li_&]:mt-1 [li_&]:gap-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ul]:pb-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ol]:pb-1 list-disc flex flex-col gap-1 pl-8 mb-3
ul.li: One person builds the Flutter UI in Dart
Another builds the Mastra agent workflow in TypeScript
Another maintains the flood prediction model in Python

div.p: Flutter talks to all of them via HTTP calls — they never need to touch each other's code.
Want me to start writing the Dart files now?

ul.li: Screen background → frost
Cards and surfaces → white
All primary buttons → deep with white text
Top nav bar → navy with sky text
Body text → ink on frost (highest contrast: 12:1)
Never put ocean blue text on white — it only just passes AA so save it for large buttons only
Risk badges always use white text — all three semantic colors pass AA

iframe.title: visualize: Floodaid app icon
iframe.style: width: 100%; border-width: medium; border-style: none; border-color: currentcolor; border-image: initial; background-color: transparent; height: 470px;

div.p: That's Droppy — your FloodAid mascot as a proper iOS app icon. The design follows Apple's icon guidelines:

ul.class: [li_&]:mb-0 [li_&]:mt-1 [li_&]:gap-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ul]:pb-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ol]:pb-1 list-disc flex flex-col gap-1 pl-8 mb-3
ul.li: Square with iOS rounded corners (superellipse rx="40")
1024×1024 master at the top, then scaled down to 120, 80, 58, and 40px
At small sizes the hat and feet drop out naturally, keeping just the face readable
Blue gradient background, orange rain hat, big expressive eyes

div.p: To use it in Flutter, save the SVG as a PNG at 1024×1024 and drop it into assets/icon/icon.png, then add the flutter_launcher_icons package to auto-generate all the required iOS sizes.
